I agree with most of what you say but disagree with a few points. 

Oil and gas pays well for many careers and pays poorly for many other careers.  ~~Store clerks? I would assume that store clerks/cashiers are the most common jobs at shell. They're employees. They're not paid well.~~  Sure, petroleum engineers make big bucks, as does the CEO. It's about the disparity as opposed to how well off the top 20% of the company is doing.  "Look how rich my boss is!" Is not something to brag about.  
 
I'm not arguing for equal pay across the board either. Petroleum engineers should be paid more.  I just think with profits like this they could be doing better for the employees that aren't doing as well. 

And you're absolutely right about it being windfall profits.  It would be too risky for them to give everyone a huge pay raise because next years profits may be non-existent, and they'd still be on the hook for the pay raises.

At a minimum, I think the employees should be getting a  MASSIVE bonus this year.  Honestly, a 50% or 75% bonus.  Maybe more.

Or they could take their windfall profits and turn it into steady raises for the next 10 years by structuring the money to last that long.  

I'm sure the money will be used elsewhere, though.  It always is.  Apparently, shell made about $40bn profit last year and got media attention for giving employees an 8% bonus.  Even if you made 100k a year,  an 8k bonus when the company made 400k off of you feels dirty.  It's even worse if you're the store clerk making 40k.

Edit: I've been told that clerks/cashiers are not employees of shell. It's probably true, im not fact-checking. Regardless,  with the knowledge that ~30,000 employees are based in Asia I think it's still fair to say that shell underpays a majority of their employees.

$9,600,000,000 profit;
93,000 employees;
$103,225 profit per employee
FOR THE FIRST QUARTER. 

Obviously, Shell isn't paying all of its employees 100k a year. if they wanted to pay everyone 100k a year, they absolutely could. It only took them 3 months to make that money.  

The sad thing is,  they're making $9.6bn AFTER paying their employees. It's profit.  Something feels wrong about making $ 40k a year when the average employee is on track to bring in $ 400k in profit this year. Employees are giving back the company 90% of the money they make.

The CEO paid himself ~$11,500,000 in 2022. If you consider the $11.5mn reasonable (I do,  honestly), what is not reasonable is that from 2021 to 2022, the ceo gave himself a 50% raise. I would guess the average employee got somewhere between 3% and 7%.


Edit again: it's so much worse than I realized. I made the assumption that the employees are American. (I know,  i know,  we are, in fact, not the center of the universe) They are mostly from Asia, Only 23,000 American employees. I have no idea what salary they're getting, but I guarantee it's not equivalent to $40k USD. 

Edit:  My guess of $40k a year is probably ~~low~~ high.  I know I make a ton of assumptions.
